chapter.title: Operating systems
chapter.summary: What the kernel does for your program: processes, threads, scheduling, memory, and the hard parts of concurrency.

lessons.title: Processes, threads and CPU scheduling
lessons.summary: What a process and a thread really are, how the kernel switches between them, the main scheduling algorithms, and the cost of context switches.

parts.label: Processes
parts.body:
## The operating system's job

An operating system (OS) does three things for programs: it **shares** the hardware (CPU, memory, disk, network) fairly among many programs, it **isolates** them so one buggy program cannot corrupt another, and it **abstracts** hardware into simple interfaces (files, sockets, processes).

The **kernel** is the privileged core of the OS. Programs run in **user mode** with restricted rights; to do anything that touches hardware they make a **system call** (`read`, `write`, `fork`, `mmap`), which traps into **kernel mode**, runs the privileged code, and returns. A system call costs hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds, far more than a normal function call.

## What a process is

A **process** is a running program: code plus its own state. The OS gives each process:

- its own **virtual address space** (a private view of memory, see the memory lesson),
- one or more **threads of execution** (at least one),
- open resources: file descriptors, sockets, signal handlers,
- an identity and permissions (PID, user id).

The kernel keeps a **process control block (PCB)** for each: PID, state, saved registers, program counter, memory maps, open files, scheduling info.

Typical address-space layout (low to high addresses): **text** (code, read-only) → **data/bss** (globals) → **heap** (grows up, `malloc`) → ... → **stack** (grows down, function frames and locals).

## Process states

```
new → ready ⇄ running → terminated
          ↑      ↓
          └─ waiting (blocked on I/O, lock, sleep)
```

- **Ready**: could run, waiting for a CPU.
- **Running**: executing on a CPU core.
- **Waiting/blocked**: cannot run until something happens (disk read finishes, a packet arrives). Blocked processes do not waste CPU, which is why one core can serve thousands of connections.

## Creating processes (Unix)

- `fork()` clones the calling process; the child gets a copy of the address space (made cheap by **copy-on-write**: pages are shared until one side writes).
- `exec()` replaces the current program image with a new one. A shell runs a command with `fork` then `exec` in the child, and the parent `wait()`s.
- A child that exits but is not `wait()`ed for becomes a **zombie** (just an entry in the process table holding the exit status). If the parent dies first, the child is **orphaned** and adopted by `init`.

## Inter-process communication (IPC)

Processes are isolated, so sharing needs explicit channels: **pipes** (byte stream, `ls | grep`), **Unix domain sockets**, **network sockets**, **shared memory** (fastest; you must synchronise yourself), **message queues**, **signals** (small asynchronous notifications such as `SIGTERM`, `SIGKILL`), and files.

parts.label: Threads and context switches
parts.body:
## Threads

A **thread** is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads of one process **share** the address space (code, heap, globals, open files) but each has its **own** stack, registers and program counter.

| | process | thread |
|---|---|---|
| memory | separate address space | shared with siblings |
| creation cost | heavier (page tables, resources) | lighter |
| communication | IPC needed | read and write shared memory directly |
| failure | one crash does not affect others | a bad pointer or exception can kill the whole process |
| synchronisation | rarely | essential (locks) |

Threads give **concurrency** (making progress on several tasks) and, on multi-core hardware, **parallelism** (really running at the same instant). Concurrency is about structure, parallelism is about execution.

## Thread models

- **Kernel threads (1:1)**: each user thread maps to a kernel thread scheduled by the OS (Linux pthreads, Java platform threads). True parallelism, blocking calls only block that thread, but each costs memory (a stack of ~1 MB reserved) and a kernel object.
- **User-level / green threads (M:N)**: a runtime multiplexes many lightweight tasks onto a few OS threads (Go goroutines, Erlang processes, Java virtual threads, Kotlin coroutines). Cheap enough for millions, but the runtime must avoid blocking the carrier thread.
- **Event loop**: one thread plus non-blocking I/O (Node.js, nginx). Great for I/O-bound work, bad for CPU-bound work on that thread.

## Context switch

When the scheduler switches the CPU from one thread to another it: saves the running thread's registers and program counter into its control block, picks another, loads its saved state, and (for a different process) switches the **address space**, which invalidates cached translations in the **TLB**.

The direct cost is a few microseconds, but the **indirect cost** is bigger: CPU caches and the TLB are now full of the previous thread's data (**cache pollution**), so the next thread starts slowly. This is why a server with 10,000 busy threads performs worse than one with a thread per core and async I/O, and why you size pools instead of spawning without limit.

## Multithreading pitfalls

- **Race condition**: result depends on the unlucky timing of interleaved accesses to shared data (next lesson).
- **Thread-per-request** exhausts memory under load; use pools, async I/O, or lightweight threads.
- **Thread-local storage** gives each thread its own copy of a variable (useful for per-request context).
- Blocking calls inside a small thread pool can starve it ("thread pool starvation") while the CPU is idle.

parts.label: Scheduling
parts.body:
## What the scheduler optimises

When more threads are ready than there are cores, the scheduler decides who runs. Goals conflict, so every scheduler is a trade-off between:

- **Throughput**: jobs completed per second.
- **Turnaround time**: submit → finish.
- **Waiting time**: time spent in the ready queue.
- **Response time**: submit → first output (what interactive users feel).
- **Fairness** and **no starvation**.
- **CPU utilisation**.

Schedulers are **preemptive** (the OS can take the CPU away, using timer interrupts) or **non-preemptive** (a task runs until it blocks or finishes). Modern general-purpose OSes are preemptive.

## Classic algorithms

| algorithm | idea | strength | weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FCFS** | first come, first served | trivial, no starvation | **convoy effect**: one long job delays all short ones |
| **SJF / SRTF** | run the shortest (remaining) job first | provably minimal average waiting time | needs to know burst length; long jobs can **starve** |
| **Round robin** | each task gets a time slice (quantum), then goes to the back | good response time, fair | too small a quantum wastes time switching; too large degrades into FCFS |
| **Priority** | highest priority first | important work first | starvation; fix with **aging** (priority rises while waiting) and avoid priority inversion |
| **Multilevel feedback queue** | several queues; new jobs high priority, CPU hogs sink to lower queues | approximates SJF without knowing burst times; favours interactive tasks | complex to tune |

**Priority inversion**: a low-priority thread holds a lock that a high-priority thread needs, while a medium-priority thread keeps preempting the low one. The famous Mars Pathfinder resets were caused by this. Fix: **priority inheritance** (the holder temporarily gets the waiter's priority).

Linux's default scheduler, **CFS** (and the newer EEVDF), tracks how much CPU time each task has received and always runs the one that has had the least, weighted by `nice` value; real-time classes (`SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR`) take priority over it.

## Worked example: round robin vs FCFS

Three jobs arrive at time 0 with CPU bursts: A = 24, B = 3, C = 3.

- **FCFS** (order A, B, C): waits are A=0, B=24, C=27. Average = **17**.
- **Round robin, quantum 4**: A runs 0-4, B 4-7 (done), C 7-10 (done), A resumes 10-30. Waits (finish minus burst): B=7-3=4, C=10-3=7, A=30-24=6. Average ≈ **5.7**.

Round robin finishes the short jobs far earlier, which is why interactive systems prefer it; the cost is a few extra context switches.

## CPU-bound vs I/O-bound

I/O-bound tasks use brief CPU bursts and then block; they deserve quick access to the CPU when ready (interactive responsiveness). CPU-bound tasks use full quanta. Good schedulers boost the former and tax the latter, which is exactly what a multilevel feedback queue does.

  W -->|"event completes"| R

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

OS questions check whether you have a **mental model of what the machine is doing** beneath your framework: why threads are cheaper than processes, what a context switch costs, and how scheduling choices show up as latency.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What is the difference between a process and a thread?

**Model answer.** A process is an isolated instance of a program with its own address space and resources. A thread is an execution path inside a process; threads share the process's memory and open files but have their own stack and registers. Threads are cheaper to create and switch and can share data directly, but a bug in one thread can corrupt or crash the whole process, and shared data needs synchronisation. Processes give isolation at the cost of IPC and heavier switching.

### 2. What happens during a context switch and why is it expensive?

**Model answer.** The kernel saves the current thread's registers and program counter, selects another thread, and restores its state, switching address spaces if it belongs to a different process, which flushes TLB entries. The direct cost is microseconds, but the larger hidden cost is cache and TLB pollution, since the new thread's working set is cold. That is why too many runnable threads hurt throughput and why servers use pools or async I/O.

### 3. Explain concurrency versus parallelism.

**Model answer.** Concurrency means managing multiple tasks whose lifetimes overlap, possibly by interleaving on one core; parallelism means executing multiple tasks at the same instant on multiple cores. A single-threaded event loop is concurrent but not parallel. You need parallelism for CPU-bound speed-ups and concurrency for I/O-bound responsiveness.

### 4. Compare round robin and shortest job first.

**Model answer.** SJF minimises average waiting time but needs burst estimates and can starve long jobs. Round robin gives each task a fixed time slice, guaranteeing fairness and good response time, at the cost of switching overhead and worse average turnaround for equal-length jobs. The quantum is the lever: too small wastes time switching, too big degenerates into FCFS. Real systems use multilevel feedback queues to approximate SJF by observing behaviour.

### 5. What is a zombie process and how do you avoid it?

**Model answer.** A child that has exited but whose parent hasn't collected its exit status with `wait()`/`waitpid()`. It holds only a process-table entry, but enough of them can exhaust PIDs. Avoid by having the parent wait (or ignore `SIGCHLD`), or by double-forking so `init` adopts the grandchild. In containers, run a proper init (`tini`, `--init`) as PID 1 so orphans are reaped.

### 6. What is priority inversion and how is it fixed?

**Model answer.** A high-priority task blocks on a lock held by a low-priority task, while medium-priority tasks keep the low-priority task from running, so effectively the high-priority task waits on the medium ones. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder to the waiter's priority so it can finish and release the lock.

## Rapid-fire

- **What does `fork` + copy-on-write buy?** Cheap process creation by sharing pages until written.
- **Do threads share the stack?** No, each has its own; heap and globals are shared.
- **What is the convoy effect?** Short jobs stuck behind a long one in FCFS.
- **System call vs function call?** A system call crosses into kernel mode and is much costlier.
- **What is preemption?** The OS taking the CPU from a running task, usually via a timer interrupt.

keyPoints: A process is an isolated program instance with its own address space; a thread is an execution path sharing its process's memory but with its own stack and registers.
System calls move from user mode to kernel mode; context switches save and restore registers and pollute caches and the TLB.
Concurrency is overlapping tasks; parallelism is running simultaneously on multiple cores.
FCFS suffers the convoy effect; SJF minimises waiting but starves; round robin is fair; multilevel feedback queues approximate SJF in practice.
Avoid zombies by waiting on children; fix priority inversion with priority inheritance.

check.q: Which resource do threads of the same process NOT share?
check.why: Each thread needs its own stack to hold its call frames and local variables, while heap, globals and file descriptors are shared.

options: The CPU runs slower with more threads
Context switches and cache/TLB pollution consume time that would do useful work
check.q: Why can adding more and more runnable threads reduce throughput?
check.why: Frequent switching costs direct time and destroys cache locality, so beyond a point more threads means more overhead.

options: Short jobs waiting behind one long job in FCFS scheduling
check.q: What does the convoy effect describe?
check.why: In first-come-first-served scheduling a long CPU-bound job delays every short job queued behind it, raising average waiting time.

lessons.title: Virtual memory: paging, TLB and page replacement
lessons.summary: How each process gets a private address space, how page tables and the TLB translate addresses, what a page fault does, and how the OS chooses pages to evict.

parts.label: Address spaces and paging
parts.body:
## The problem virtual memory solves

Physical RAM is a shared, finite array of bytes. Without help, programs would need to know where they sit in RAM, could overwrite each other, and could never use more memory than is installed. **Virtual memory** gives every process the illusion of a **huge, private, contiguous address space** (for example 128 TiB on 64-bit Linux), and the hardware plus OS silently map it onto whatever physical memory is available.

Benefits:

1. **Isolation**: a process cannot even name another process's memory.
2. **Simplicity**: every program is compiled assuming the same layout.
3. **Overcommit**: the address space can exceed RAM; unused parts live on disk (swap) or are not backed at all.
4. **Sharing**: the same physical page can be mapped into many processes (shared libraries, copy-on-write after `fork`, shared memory).
5. **Protection**: each page has permissions (read, write, execute, user/kernel).

## Pages and frames

Memory is divided into fixed-size blocks: **pages** (virtual) and **frames** (physical), typically **4 KiB** (also 2 MiB / 1 GiB "huge pages"). A virtual address splits into:

```
virtual address = [ virtual page number (VPN) | page offset ]
```

The offset (low 12 bits for 4 KiB pages) is unchanged by translation. The **VPN** is looked up in the process's **page table** to find the **physical frame number**:

```
physical address = [ frame number | same offset ]
```

Worked example with 4 KiB pages: virtual address `0x1A2B3C`. Offset = low 12 bits = `0xB3C`. VPN = `0x1A2`. If the page table maps page `0x1A2` to frame `0x7F`, the physical address is `0x7F000 + 0xB3C = 0x7FB3C`.

## Page tables

A page table entry (PTE) holds: the frame number, a **present** bit (is it in RAM?), **dirty** bit (modified?), **accessed** bit (recently used?), and permission bits (R/W/X, user/supervisor).

A flat table for a 48-bit address space would have 2³⁶ entries (hundreds of GB), so real systems use **multi-level page tables** (4 or 5 levels on x86-64): a tree where unused regions simply have no lower-level tables, so only the parts of the address space actually in use cost memory.

The catch: every memory access would need several extra memory reads just to translate the address.

## The TLB

The **Translation Lookaside Buffer** is a tiny, very fast cache of recent VPN → frame translations inside the CPU (tens to thousands of entries). A **TLB hit** adds almost no cost; a **TLB miss** triggers a page-table walk (hardware on x86/ARM), costing roughly tens to hundreds of cycles.

- Programs with **locality** (accessing nearby memory repeatedly) hit the TLB almost always.
- Random access over a huge array (large hash tables, pointer chasing) misses constantly.
- **Huge pages** (2 MiB) let one TLB entry cover 512x more memory: databases and JVMs use them for speed.
- A process context switch changes the page table, so non-tagged TLB entries are flushed (modern CPUs tag entries with an address-space id, reducing this).

Effective access time = `hit_ratio × t_mem + (1 − hit_ratio) × (t_mem × levels + t_mem)`; even a 99 percent hit ratio is crucial because a miss multiplies memory cost.

parts.label: Page faults and replacement
parts.body:
## Page faults

If the PTE says **not present** (or the access violates permissions), the CPU raises a **page fault** and the kernel takes over. Causes and outcomes:

| situation | what the OS does |
|---|---|
| **Valid page, not in RAM** (swapped out, or file-backed and not loaded yet) | find a free frame (evicting another page if needed), read the page from disk, update the PTE, restart the instruction. A **major fault**: millions of cycles. |
| **Valid page, first touch of fresh memory** | allocate a zeroed frame (demand paging). A **minor fault**: microseconds. |
| **Write to a copy-on-write page** | copy the page, give the writer its private copy |
| **Invalid address / permission violation** | send `SIGSEGV` (segmentation fault) and usually kill the process |

**Demand paging**: pages are loaded only when touched, so starting a 1 GB program is fast and only used pages consume RAM. `mmap` maps a file straight into the address space using the same mechanism, which is how executables, shared libraries, and many databases read data.

## Page replacement: who gets evicted?

When RAM is full, the OS must choose a **victim** frame. A good policy evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time.

| algorithm | idea | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Optimal (Belady)** | evict the page used farthest in the future | impossible to implement; the benchmark |
| **FIFO** | evict the oldest page | simple but can evict hot pages; shows **Belady's anomaly** (more frames can cause more faults) |
| **LRU** | evict the least recently used | good approximation of optimal; exact LRU needs expensive bookkeeping |
| **Clock (second chance)** | pages in a circle with an accessed bit; the hand clears bits and evicts the first page found with bit 0 | cheap approximation of LRU used in practice |
| **LFU** | evict least frequently used | can keep stale once-hot pages; needs aging |

Worked example: reference string `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5` with 3 frames. FIFO gives 9 faults; with 4 frames it gives **10** (Belady's anomaly). LRU never shows the anomaly (it is a "stack algorithm").

## Thrashing and the working set

If the total **working set** (pages actively needed) of running processes exceeds RAM, the system spends its time swapping pages in and out instead of working: **thrashing**; CPU utilisation collapses while disk is saturated. Fixes: reduce the number of running processes, add RAM, improve locality, or use the OS's working-set / OOM policies. On Linux, when memory is truly exhausted the **OOM killer** terminates a process to save the system; in containers a **cgroup memory limit** triggers the same for just that container (the dreaded "OOMKilled").

## Practical views of memory

- **RSS** (resident set size): the pages actually in RAM now. **VSZ**: the whole virtual size, mostly irrelevant.
- **Heap fragmentation** wastes memory even if the total free amount is large; allocators (jemalloc, tcmalloc) mitigate it.
- **Stack overflow**: unbounded recursion exhausts the (limited, e.g. 8 MB) stack.
- **Memory leak**: allocation never freed in manual-memory languages; in managed languages, references that keep objects reachable.
- **Memory-mapped I/O** and the **page cache**: Linux caches file data in otherwise idle RAM, so "free memory" being low is normal and healthy.

  W -->|"not present"| F["Page fault: OS loads page from disk"] --> U
  P --> M[("RAM")]

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

They want to see you can **trace an address translation**, explain why a page fault is not an error, and connect virtual memory to real symptoms: slow servers, OOM kills, swapping.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What is virtual memory and why do we have it?

**Model answer.** It gives every process its own private, contiguous address space that the hardware and OS map onto physical frames on demand. It provides isolation and protection between processes, lets programs ignore physical layout, permits an address space bigger than RAM through paging to disk, and allows efficient sharing and copy-on-write. Without it, any program could overwrite any other and memory management would be the application's problem.

### 2. Walk me through translating a virtual address.

**Model answer.** Split the address into virtual page number and offset. The MMU checks the TLB for the VPN; on a hit it combines the cached frame number with the offset. On a miss it walks the multi-level page table; if the entry is present it fills the TLB and proceeds; if not present it raises a page fault, the kernel loads the page (or allocates a zeroed one), updates the table, and restarts the instruction. The offset is never translated.

### 3. What is a page fault and is it always bad?

**Model answer.** It is a CPU exception raised when a page is not mapped or the access isn't permitted. Many are normal: minor faults from demand paging of fresh or copy-on-write pages cost microseconds; major faults requiring disk I/O are expensive and slow the process visibly. Only invalid accesses end in a segmentation fault. High major-fault rates indicate memory pressure.

### 4. What is thrashing and how do you address it?

**Model answer.** When processes' combined working sets exceed physical memory, the system continuously evicts pages that are needed immediately, so most time goes to paging I/O and useful work collapses. Reduce concurrency, add memory, improve locality or cap memory per workload. In containers, set realistic limits so the OOM killer acts on one container rather than the host swapping.

### 5. Why does the TLB matter for performance?

**Model answer.** Every memory access needs a translation. The TLB caches recent ones, making translation nearly free; a miss costs a multi-level page walk, which is several additional memory accesses. Programs with poor locality, such as random access across huge data, suffer TLB misses, so techniques like contiguous layouts, blocking, and huge pages improve speed.

### 6. LRU versus Clock versus FIFO?

**Model answer.** FIFO ignores recency and can evict hot pages and exhibit Belady's anomaly. LRU evicts the least recently used page and approximates optimal behaviour, but exact tracking is costly in hardware. Clock keeps a circular list with an accessed bit, giving pages a second chance, approximating LRU cheaply, which is why real kernels use variants of it.

## Rapid-fire

- **Page size?** Typically 4 KiB; huge pages 2 MiB.
- **What does `fork` use to stay cheap?** Copy-on-write.
- **Segfault cause?** Invalid or forbidden memory access.
- **What is demand paging?** Loading pages only when first touched.
- **Why is "free memory low" often fine on Linux?** The page cache uses spare RAM and is reclaimable.

keyPoints: Virtual memory gives each process a private address space mapped onto physical frames, enabling isolation, protection, sharing and overcommit.
A virtual address is a page number plus an unchanged offset; multi-level page tables and a TLB make translation affordable.
A page fault is an exception: minor ones are normal demand paging or copy-on-write, major ones need disk I/O, invalid ones become SIGSEGV.
Replacement policies: optimal is the benchmark, FIFO can show Belady's anomaly, LRU is good, Clock approximates it cheaply.
Thrashing happens when working sets exceed RAM; the OOM killer or cgroup limits end memory exhaustion.

check.q: A virtual address is 0x1A2B3C with 4 KiB pages. What is the page offset?
check.why: 4 KiB pages use the low 12 bits for the offset, which are 0xB3C. The remaining bits, 0x1A2, are the virtual page number.

options: A page-table walk to find the translation
check.q: What does a TLB miss cause?
check.why: A TLB miss only means the translation is not cached; the hardware walks the page table. A disk read happens only if the page is also not present in RAM.

check.q: Which policy can produce more faults when given more frames?
check.why: This is Belady's anomaly, which affects FIFO but not stack algorithms like LRU and optimal.

lessons.title: Synchronisation, race conditions and deadlocks
lessons.summary: Why shared mutable state breaks, mutexes, semaphores, condition variables, atomics, the four deadlock conditions and how to avoid, detect and recover from them.

parts.label: Race conditions and locks
parts.body:
## Why concurrency is hard

Single-threaded code is deterministic: statements run in program order. Once two threads touch **shared mutable state**, the result depends on how their instructions interleave, which the OS decides unpredictably. Bugs appear only sometimes ("works on my machine"), vanish under a debugger, and come back in production.

## A race condition, step by step

`counter++` looks atomic but compiles to three steps: **load** counter into a register, **add** 1, **store** back.

| time | thread A | thread B | counter in memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | load → 5 | | 5 |
| 2 | | load → 5 | 5 |
| 3 | add → 6 | add → 6 | 5 |
| 4 | store 6 | | 6 |
| 5 | | store 6 | **6** (should be 7: one update lost) |

A **race condition** is any situation where correctness depends on timing. A **data race** is the specific case of two threads accessing the same memory concurrently, at least one writing, with no synchronisation; in languages like C, C++ and Rust it is undefined behaviour, and in Java and Go it breaks guarantees.

The code that must not interleave is a **critical section**. Requirements for a good solution: **mutual exclusion** (one at a time), **progress** (if nobody is inside, someone who wants in gets in), **bounded waiting** (no starvation).

## Tools

**Mutex (lock):** `lock()` before the critical section, `unlock()` after. Only one holder at a time; others block. Always release in a `finally`/RAII/`defer` so exceptions cannot leave it locked. Keep critical sections **short** and never do I/O while holding a hot lock.

**Spinlock:** busy-waits instead of sleeping. Only sensible for very short sections on multi-core, in kernels.

**Read-write lock:** many concurrent readers or one writer; helps read-heavy data but writers can starve.

**Semaphore:** a counter with `acquire` (wait, decrement) and `release` (signal, increment). A **binary** semaphore resembles a mutex; a **counting** semaphore limits access to N resources (a pool of 10 connections).

**Condition variable / monitor:** lets a thread **wait until a condition holds** while releasing the associated mutex. Always re-check the condition in a `while` loop, because of spurious wake-ups and because another thread may have changed it between the signal and your wake-up.

**Atomics and lock-free:** hardware instructions like **compare-and-swap (CAS)** update one word atomically: `if (x == expected) x = new`. `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet`, `Atomics.add` use it. Lock-free structures retry on contention instead of blocking, avoiding deadlock but are subtle (the **ABA problem**: a value changes A → B → A, and CAS wrongly succeeds).

**Memory model:** compilers and CPUs reorder operations and cache values per core. Without synchronisation one thread may never see another's write, or see writes out of order. Locks, `volatile` (Java), atomics, and channels establish **happens-before** relationships that make writes visible. Don't rely on "it seems to work".

**Better than locking:** share less. Prefer **immutability**, **message passing** (channels, actors, queues: "do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating"), **thread confinement** (data owned by one thread), and concurrent data structures from the standard library.

parts.label: Classic problems
parts.body:
## Producer-consumer (bounded buffer)

Producers add items to a fixed-size buffer; consumers remove them. Producers must wait when it is full, consumers when it is empty, and access must be exclusive. With semaphores: `empty` (counts free slots, starts at N), `full` (counts items, starts at 0) and a mutex around the buffer operations. In practice use a **blocking queue** (`BlockingQueue`, Go channel, `queue.Queue`).

## Readers-writers

Many readers may read together; writers need exclusive access. Reader-preference starves writers; writer-preference starves readers; a fair lock queues arrivals.

## Dining philosophers

Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks; each needs the two adjacent forks to eat. If all grab their left fork at once, everyone waits forever for the right: **deadlock**. It models resource contention in general. Solutions: impose an order on acquiring forks (lowest number first), allow at most four to sit, or use an arbitrator.

## Deadlock

A set of threads is **deadlocked** when each waits for a resource held by another in the set, so none can proceed.

```
Thread 1: lock(A); lock(B); ...        Thread 2: lock(B); lock(A); ...
        holds A, waits for B                holds B, waits for A
```

### The four Coffman conditions (all must hold)

1. **Mutual exclusion**: resources can't be shared.
2. **Hold and wait**: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
3. **No preemption**: resources can't be forcibly taken away.
4. **Circular wait**: a cycle of threads each waiting for the next.

### Handling deadlocks

| approach | how | trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Prevention** | break one condition: the most practical is **lock ordering** (always acquire locks in one global order), which kills circular wait | requires discipline across the codebase |
| **Avoidance** | grant a request only if the system stays in a **safe state** (Banker's algorithm) | needs maximum needs in advance; rare in practice |
| **Detection and recovery** | build a wait-for graph, find cycles, abort or roll back a victim (databases do this) | some work is lost |
| **Ignore it** (ostrich) | restart when it happens | what many general-purpose OSes do for user-space locks |

Practical rules: acquire multiple locks in a fixed order; use `tryLock` with a **timeout** and back off; don't call unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock; keep lock scopes small; prefer one coarse lock over many fine ones until profiling says otherwise.

### Related liveness failures

- **Livelock**: threads keep reacting to each other and make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor); fix with randomised back-off.
- **Starvation**: a thread never gets the resource because others always win.
- **Priority inversion**: see the scheduling lesson.

## Worked example: why lock ordering works

Transfer money between accounts. Naive: lock `from`, then lock `to`. Transfers A→B and B→A running together deadlock. Fix: always lock the account with the **smaller id first**, regardless of direction. Then every thread acquires in the same order, so no cycle can form.

code.source:
# Condition variable: wait in a while loop, never an if
import threading
from collections import deque

class BoundedBuffer:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.q, self.cap = deque(), cap
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(self.lock)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(self.lock)

    def put(self, x):
        with self.not_full:
            while len(self.q) >= self.cap:        # re-check after every wake-up
                self.not_full.wait()
            self.q.append(x)
            self.not_empty.notify()

    def get(self):
        with self.not_empty:
            while not self.q:
                self.not_empty.wait()
            x = self.q.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()
            return x

parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Concurrency questions are about **precise reasoning under interleaving**. A strong answer names the exact failure (lost update, deadlock cycle), the invariant that must hold, and the lightest mechanism that protects it.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What is a race condition? Give an example.

**Model answer.** A bug where the outcome depends on the relative timing of threads. `counter++` is load, add, store; if two threads load the same value before either stores, one increment is lost. Fix by making the read-modify-write atomic with a lock or atomic operation, or by avoiding shared mutable state.

### 2. Mutex versus semaphore?

**Model answer.** A mutex enforces mutual exclusion and has ownership: the thread that locked it must unlock it. A semaphore is a counter used for signalling and for limiting access to N resources, with no ownership: any thread can release it. A binary semaphore is similar to a mutex but lacks ownership and priority-inheritance semantics, so for protecting a critical section I use a mutex; for resource pools or signalling between threads, a semaphore.

### 3. What are the four conditions for deadlock, and how would you prevent it in code?

**Model answer.** Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait must all hold. The practical prevention is eliminating circular wait by defining a global lock order and always acquiring locks in that order, e.g. by account id. Others: acquire all locks at once, use `tryLock` with timeouts and back off, or reduce lock count by redesigning around message passing or a single owner thread.

### 4. Why must you wait on a condition variable in a loop?

**Model answer.** Because of spurious wake-ups and because the condition can change between being signalled and reacquiring the mutex (another consumer may have taken the item). Re-checking the predicate in a `while` loop guarantees correctness; an `if` can proceed with a false condition.

### 5. What is the difference between a deadlock and a livelock?

**Model answer.** In a deadlock threads are blocked forever waiting on each other and consume no CPU. In a livelock they keep running, repeatedly responding to each other's actions, but make no progress. Livelocks are mitigated with randomised back-off or arbitration.

### 6. Explain compare-and-swap and the ABA problem.

**Model answer.** CAS atomically sets a memory location to a new value only if it currently equals an expected value, returning whether it succeeded; loops around CAS implement lock-free updates. ABA occurs when the value changes from A to B and back to A between the read and the CAS, so the CAS succeeds even though the state changed in between, which can corrupt lock-free structures like stacks. Solutions include version counters (tagged pointers) or hazard pointers.

### 7. How do you debug a hung production service you suspect is deadlocked?

**Model answer.** Take thread dumps (`jstack`, `kill -3`, `pprof goroutine`, `py-spy dump`) a few seconds apart and look for threads blocked on locks, then trace the holder and waiters to find the cycle. Confirm CPU is idle (deadlock) rather than high (livelock/spin). Fix with consistent lock ordering or timeouts, add lock-acquisition timeouts and metrics, and add a race detector or deadlock detector in tests.

## Rapid-fire

- **Which is safer to share: immutable or mutable data?** Immutable.
- **Does `volatile` make `count++` atomic?** No; it gives visibility, not atomicity.
- **What breaks circular wait?** A global lock ordering.
- **What detects data races?** ThreadSanitizer, `go run -race`.
- **What does a counting semaphore model?** A pool of N identical resources.

keyPoints: A race condition is timing-dependent correctness; counter++ is load, add and store, so concurrent updates can be lost without atomicity.
Use mutexes for critical sections, semaphores for counting resources, condition variables (in a while loop) for waiting, and atomics for single-word updates.
Prefer sharing less: immutability, message passing and thread confinement beat clever locking.
Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; global lock ordering is the practical cure.
Diagnose hangs with repeated thread dumps; livelock burns CPU, deadlock does not.
